edition.deck: Ukraine’s president challenges Washington’s approach to peace talks as fresh figures, election uncertainty and European divisions shape the day.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and consequential reporting. Returning stories from the previous edition are omitted where this gather adds no material update; related coverage is grouped where it reports the same underlying event.

content.headline: Zelensky says US focus on Middle East is delaying vital missiles for Ukraine
content.shortHeadline: Zelensky says US focus is delaying vital missiles for Ukraine
content.standfirst: In a BBC interview, Ukraine’s president says delays in Patriot deliveries are costing lives and urges Washington to press Russia harder in peace talks. He says negotiations are expected to resume in December.

image.caption: Volodymyr Zelensky during his BBC interview in Kyiv.

sources.originalTitle: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC

segments.body: Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine urgently needs the US to push Russia harder in peace talks and speed up deliveries of Patriot air-defence missiles. He told the BBC that a shortage of interceptors puts lives at risk as Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities grow more frequent and deadly.

segments.title: A difficult winter ahead
segments.body: Zelensky said talks mediated in Abu Dhabi made no obvious progress, and he was unsure whether European negotiators would be included in the next round. Russia, he said, appeared to have returned to its initial hardline positions. Talks are expected to resume in December.

Ukraine is bracing for a dangerous winter, he said, with attacks on Kyiv’s bridges, power cuts and strikes on logistics weighing on residents and businesses. Zelensky said Ukraine’s forces can destroy about 70% of Russia’s fastest drones, but described the shortage of ballistic-missile interceptors as “very, very big”.

content.headline: Leaked Russian records point to huge war deaths, but the totals remain uncertain
content.shortHeadline: Leaked records suggest enormous Russian war losses
content.standfirst: Analyses of data attributed to Russia’s statistics agency suggest hundreds of thousands of Russian military deaths. The records have not been independently verified, and estimates vary depending on how missing and delayed reports are counted.

image.caption: A Russian cemetery.

sources.originalTitle: Læk afslører enorme tabstal – så længe overlever en russisk soldat ved fronten
Hvad betaler russerne for krigen i Ukraine? Et hackerangreb på russisk data har givet et bud

segments.body: Russian opposition outlets Mediazona and Meduza say leaked data from Rosstat points to about 490,000 Russian soldiers killed by September 2026. Their estimate rises above 720,000 when delayed registrations and soldiers reported missing who are presumed dead are included. Rosstat says it was hacked but denies that data was stolen.

segments.title: What the figures can—and cannot—show
segments.body: The data was reportedly obtained after pro-Ukrainian hacker groups accessed Rosstat servers. DR’s analysis of the leak says categories do not always distinguish combatants from civilians, while death registrations can be delayed. TV 2 reports that the figures are estimates, not an officially confirmed count.

The two Danish reports draw on overlapping leaked material but give different totals and explain the calculations differently. The Russian government has not confirmed a death toll; the available evidence cannot establish a definitive figure.

perspectives.body: DR’s account highlights a key limitation: some leaked death categories may include civilians, and the figures can lag because deaths are registered late. Its cited analysis says distinguishing combatants from civilians may be difficult or impossible in some cases.

content.headline: Only 24 EU states back proposed €45bn loan for Ukraine
content.shortHeadline: EU support for a €45bn Ukraine loan falls short of unanimity
content.standfirst: Germany’s chancellor called for all member states to contribute, but only 24 backed the European Commission’s proposed loan at Thursday’s summit. Bulgaria would join only its non-military portion; talks are due to continue in December.

image.caption: EU leaders António Costa and Andrej Babiš at a summit.

sources.originalTitle: Kun 24 EU-lande stiller sig bag Ukraine-lån på topmøde

segments.body: Only 24 of the EU’s 27 member states supported a European Commission proposal for a €45bn loan to Ukraine at Thursday’s summit, European Council president António Costa said. Bulgaria would take part only in the non-military portion, with support focused on Ukrainian regions that have a Bulgarian minority.

segments.title: A decision deferred
segments.body: Germany’s Friedrich Merz had called for all EU countries to contribute. Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia had already opted out of a previous Ukraine loan; Bulgaria has now also limited its participation. Costa said negotiations were not over and leaders would return to the issue at their December summit.

content.headline: Hasina’s planned return to Bangladesh puts Dhaka and Delhi on edge
content.shortHeadline: Hasina’s proposed return raises tensions for Bangladesh and India
content.standfirst: The ousted Bangladeshi leader says she plans to return on 16 December, despite a death sentence in a trial held in her absence and a government promise to arrest her. The announcement also sharpens tensions with India, where she is staying.

image.caption: Sheikh Hasina with Narendra Modi in Delhi in 2024.

sources.originalTitle: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind

segments.body: Sheikh Hasina’s spokesperson says the ousted prime minister plans to return to Bangladesh on 16 December, the anniversary of the country’s 1971 victory over Pakistan. Hasina fled to Delhi in 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule. Bangladesh’s government says she would be arrested if she returned.

segments.title: A political and diplomatic test
segments.body: Hasina was sentenced to death in a trial held in her absence after being convicted of crimes against humanity linked to the crackdown on the uprising. India says her extradition request is being examined through its established process. The BBC reports that her announcement could deepen unrest and complicate relations between Dhaka and Delhi; whether she will actually return remains uncertain.

content.headline: Taiwan votes amid warnings of alleged Chinese election interference
content.shortHeadline: Taiwan votes as officials warn of alleged Chinese interference
content.standfirst: Local elections on Saturday will test Taiwan’s ruling party, with officials warning of suspected disinformation and harassment linked to Beijing. China rejects the allegations, while voters are also weighing housing, wages and other local concerns.

image.caption: Democratic Progressive Party mayoral candidate Puma Shen greets supporters at a rally.

sources.originalTitle: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections

segments.body: Taiwanese voters choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts on Saturday. The races are largely about local issues, but officials have raised concerns about thousands of suspected cases of misinformation or election interference, including reports of China-linked AI-generated videos targeting politicians.

segments.title: Local races, wider stakes
segments.body: China calls the interference allegations fabricated. Political scientist Wei-Ting Yen told the Guardian that the results could still affect cross-strait relations. The ruling Democratic Progressive party faces the Kuomintang, which supports closer ties with Beijing; China claims Taiwan as its territory and has not ruled out using force.

Economic concerns are also prominent. Taiwan’s economy has grown rapidly amid the global AI boom, but the reporting notes stagnant wages and high housing costs, and some voters question the scale of proposed defence spending. Local results may shape the parties’ prospects ahead of the 2028 presidential election, but are not a direct measure of national support.

content.headline: Thanksgiving storm disrupts US travel as outages near one million
content.shortHeadline: Storm disrupts US Thanksgiving travel and leaves many without power
content.standfirst: Flooding, damaging winds and high tides disrupted travel across the US, with more than 400 flights cancelled and nearly one million households reporting outages on Thursday evening. Officials warned some repairs could take days.

image.caption: Storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North America.

sources.originalTitle: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US

segments.body: A powerful storm brought heavy rain, winds and coastal flooding to the eastern US on Thanksgiving, while Pacific storms and high tides affected the West Coast. FlightAware reported more than 400 cancellations and 2,200 delays on Thursday; almost one million households were without power by evening.

segments.title: Emergency measures and travel warnings
segments.body: New Jersey and New York declared states of emergency, and organisers postponed New York’s Macy’s Thanksgiving parade until Saturday. Flooding affected communities and airport runways, while authorities warned that power restoration could take days in some areas. California coastal rail services also cancelled trains because of high tides.

content.headline: New Zealand’s governing coalition needs a deal after final election count
content.shortHeadline: New Zealand coalition falls one seat short after final count
content.standfirst: Special votes left the National-led bloc with 65 seats in a 130-seat parliament, one short of a majority. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is beginning talks with the centrist Opportunity party, whose leader says her party’s policy demands are non-negotiable.

image.caption: New Zealand prime minister Christopher Luxon’s coalition has lost its majority.

sources.originalTitle: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat

segments.body: New Zealand’s final election count leaves the National-led coalition with 65 seats, one short of the 66 needed for a majority. National lost two seats on special votes, while Labour has 36, the Greens 17, ACT 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pāti Māori five.

segments.title: Opportunity holds the balance
segments.body: Luxon says formal negotiations will begin with the Opportunity party as well as his existing coalition partners, and warned that discussions could take time. Leader Qiulae Wong says her party will negotiate with National but will not compromise on its stated priorities, which include climate and environmental policy and a cap on political donations.

A recount could change the numbers in some electorates, but the National-led bloc currently has no majority. If negotiations fail, another election may be needed. Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party won the largest share of the party vote but lacked the numbers to form a government.

content.headline: Trump’s proposed tariffs face legal scrutiny and a changing trade landscape
content.shortHeadline: Trump’s latest tariffs face legal and political hurdles
content.standfirst: The proposed duties are not due to take effect before January or February and remain subject to consultation. Meanwhile, countries have rerouted trade, and the tariff plans face legal challenges and possible resistance in Congress.

image.caption: Donald Trump unveiled his “Liberation Day” import tariffs in 2025.

sources.originalTitle: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
Why Trump still wants his illegal ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs

segments.body: The latest US tariff proposals are presented by BBC analysis as a more tentative process than last year’s sudden announcement: rates are upper limits, subject to negotiation, and are not expected to take effect before January or possibly February. The UK is not included in this new proposal, though existing US tariffs still apply to some UK goods.

segments.title: Disputes over the legal basis
segments.body: The administration says the proposed duties respond to excess manufacturing capacity and has named 14 economies, including the EU, China and India. The EU disputes the legal premise, while China says overcapacity is a false issue. The i Paper reports that the proposals follow the Supreme Court’s rejection of an earlier emergency justification; separate tariffs are also facing legal challenges.

Trade has already shifted: BBC analysis says China’s exports to destinations outside the US have grown as its US exports fell, while Canada’s exports beyond the US rose. The wider effects for UK firms are uncertain: experts cited by The i Paper see both possible gains and risks for British exporters.

perspectives.body: The i Paper adds that some UK exporters could benefit if EU goods face higher US duties, but British suppliers of parts used in EU exports could lose out. It also cites an economist who expects no major knock-on effects for the UK.

content.headline: UK net migration falls to 77,000, the lowest since 1997 outside the pandemic
content.shortHeadline: Net migration falls to 77,000, lowest since 1997 outside Covid
content.standfirst: Official figures show net migration fell 62% in the year to June 2026, as fewer people arrived for work, study and asylum. Ministers and opposition figures dispute which government’s policies deserve the credit.

image.caption: Official figures put UK net migration at 77,000 in the year to June 2026.

sources.originalTitle: Net migration to UK falls to lowest level since 1997 excluding pandemic
UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
How much of the sharp fall in UK immigration is due to Labour’s policies?

segments.body: Net migration to the UK was 77,000 in the year to June 2026, down from 204,000 the previous year and a peak of 944,000 in 2023, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics. The total is the lowest since 1997 outside the Covid travel restrictions. An estimated 738,000 people arrived and 661,000 left.

segments.title: Why the number fell
segments.body: Fewer non-EU citizens arriving to work, study, join family or seek asylum drove the decline. Visa grants to international students and skilled workers also fell, while emigration remained relatively high. The figures show asylum arrivals fell too, and fewer people were being housed in hotels while awaiting decisions.

segments.title: Credit and caveats
segments.body: Labour says its policies restored control; the Conservatives say restrictions introduced under their government helped drive the fall. The Migration Observatory’s Madeleine Sumption says policy changes, revised statistical methods and a temporary increase in emigration all contributed, so the current level need not persist.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis stresses that the decline is not attributable to one government alone: the UK’s post-Brexit migration rules, a change in ONS methodology and the legacy of earlier high immigration all shaped the latest figures.

content.headline: Labour’s EU reset bill opens a path to closer ties, but tensions remain
content.shortHeadline: EU reset bill begins as ministers debate how far ties should go
content.standfirst: The government has begun legislation for food-trade and emissions deals with the EU, while a cabinet ally argues the reset should be only a starting point. The agreements include limits on UK voting rights and face unresolved disputes over student fees and future commitments.

image.caption: Andy Burnham with EU leaders António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels.

sources.originalTitle: Labour’s EU reset deal will be ‘floor not ceiling’, says Burnham cabinet ally
Details of two treaties at heart of Andy Burnham’s EU reset to be published
Revealed: The EU’s Brexit deal ultimatum to lock UK into youth visa scheme

segments.body: The government has introduced a bill to put parts of its EU reset into UK law, including agreements on food and drink trade and emissions trading. The food deal is not expected to take effect until 2028. Scottish secretary Douglas Alexander is set to argue that the reset should be a “floor not a ceiling” for future relations.

segments.title: What the deal provides—and what it does not
segments.body: The legal texts give the UK a consultative role in shaping some EU rules, but no final vote. The framework bill leaves scope for future agreements, while excluding a return to the single market, customs union or EU membership. The food and emissions agreements also include a ten-year termination arrangement with potential costs if either side withdraws.

segments.title: An unresolved condition
segments.body: EU diplomats cited by the Guardian say the agreements could fail to materialise without a deal on domestic-rate tuition fees for EU students within six months. UK officials deny that the issues are linked. The youth-mobility agreement’s final terms are also still to be published.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s account highlights a dispute over tuition fees: EU diplomats say progress on the wider agreements depends on a deal, while UK officials insist the matters are separate.

content.headline: Norse Atlantic suspends flights as it seeks emergency funding
content.shortHeadline: Norse Atlantic suspends flights as bankruptcy threat grows
content.standfirst: The Norwegian airline says it may file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term funding. Its suspension has disrupted UK routes and Pakistan International Airlines services, while passengers are being advised not to cancel bookings before the company’s position is clear.

sources.originalTitle: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
Norsk flyselskab er tæt på konkurs og aflyser alle flyvninger

segments.body: Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights while seeking urgent funding and discussing a possible takeover. The airline says its board intends to file for bankruptcy if no short-term solution is found. The suspension affects its UK long-haul routes and has also disrupted flights operated by Pakistan International Airlines using Norse aircraft and crews.

segments.title: Passengers face uncertainty
segments.body: Travellers told the BBC they have struggled to contact the airline or have paid more to rebook. Which? advises customers not to cancel their flights themselves while Norse has not collapsed, as doing so could affect their right to a refund. People stranded abroad are advised to contact their insurer or tour operator, depending on how they booked.

segments.title: Why the airline is in trouble
segments.body: Norse has struggled to make a profit since it was set up in 2021 and is exposed to fuel-price rises because it does not hedge its purchases. TV 2 reports that the airline told staff it had not secured the money for wages due that day. Its financial position remains uncertain while talks continue.

perspectives.body: TV 2 adds that Norse’s chief executive told staff the company could not meet a wage payment due that day, and cites a Danish investment strategist who says bondholders and lessors would rank ahead of shareholders in any rescue.

content.headline: Flu admissions rise as NHS leaders warn of winter pressure
content.shortHeadline: NHS warns flu admissions could surge as winter pressure builds
content.standfirst: Hospital admissions for flu in England have reached their highest level for this point in the year since before Covid. NHS leaders say cases may rise further in the coming days and urge eligible people to get vaccinated.

image.caption: NHS England chief executive Jim Mackey has warned of rising winter pressures.

sources.originalTitle: Hospitals in England brace for flu spike with admissions highest for time of year since pre-Covid

segments.body: Flu admissions in England rose to almost nine per 100,000 people last week, up from five the week before and the highest rate for this point in November since before Covid, according to UK Health Security Agency data. Several trusts have declared critical incidents amid winter pressures.

NHS England chief executive Jim Mackey warned that flu could rise sharply over the next five to ten days and said hospitals should consider asking staff and visitors to wear masks. Covid and RSV levels have also increased, though the agency describes them as low.

segments.title: Vaccination and capacity concerns
segments.body: The UKHSA says uptake of flu vaccination remains low, including among people with long-term health conditions. Mackey also criticised the normalisation of “corridor care”, saying it threatens patient safety and dignity as hospitals struggle to manage demand.

content.headline: UK retailers investigate after faulty goods are found at Ghana dump
content.shortHeadline: UK retailers investigate after returned goods reach Ghana dump
content.standfirst: An investigation found returned appliances bearing major UK retail labels at an Accra waste site, where workers burn and dismantle electronics. Exporting broken electrical goods is generally illegal; Tesco and Argos say they are investigating.

image.caption: Waste dumps at Agbogbloshie in Accra, Ghana.

sources.originalTitle: Faulty electrical goods returned to UK supermarkets ending up on Ghana ‘megadump’

segments.body: Faulty electrical goods bearing labels linked to Tesco and Argos were found at Agbogbloshie, a major e-waste site in Accra, according to an investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa. The report says workers burn and dismantle household items there without protective equipment. Asda referred questions to the British Retail Consortium.

segments.title: How the goods may have got there
segments.body: UK rules generally prohibit exporting broken electrical goods to Africa. The investigation says returned products can enter bulk resale and liquidation channels before being shipped abroad as second-hand goods. The Environment Agency says exports of waste electrical equipment must be notified and approved, and that no West African facilities are approved to receive British WEEE.

Tesco says it has suspended its third-party electronic-waste providers while it audits them; Argos says it is investigating how its products reached the site. A Ghanaian environmental consultant told Unearthed that exporting faulty goods shifts environmental and health costs onto local communities.

perspectives.body: The investigation includes retailers’ responses and explains a potential gap: returned items labelled “untested” can be sold through liquidation channels before anyone formally classifies them as waste.

content.headline: UK contacts 50,000 veterans to update wartime reserve records
content.shortHeadline: UK asks 50,000 veterans to update possible wartime reserve details
content.standfirst: Military chiefs are contacting veterans who may be liable for recall in an emergency, to update information on their skills and readiness. Officials say the letters are not a sign that mobilisation is imminent.

image.caption: A British veteran pictured in connection with the Strategic Reserve.

sources.originalTitle: UK brings back ‘veteran’s army’ to bolster military as Russian aggression grows
All the signs the UK is preparing for conflict on home soil
I’m a veteran living in Surrey with three kids – but I’m ready to fight Putin

segments.body: The Ministry of Defence has written to around 50,000 former service personnel to update its records on veterans who may be liable to return to the Armed Forces in an emergency. The Strategic Reserve could support regular forces and volunteer reservists, including in homeland defence.

segments.title: A reserve with unknown readiness
segments.body: The Strategic Reserve’s readiness has been allowed to lapse since the Cold War, leaving limited information about veterans’ current skills, fitness or willingness to return. The government says some may be invited to volunteer for training; a liability for recall is due to extend from age 55 to 65 when the Armed Forces Bill comes into law.

Defence analysts warn that skills may have faded and that some veterans now work in critical sectors such as health or defence. A former Army officer who received a letter told the i Paper he welcomed the effort, but the process could be costly and not all veterans may be willing to take part.

perspectives.body: Veteran Conor Wilson says the letter is welcome but argues many former service personnel may not know they remain liable for recall. He is open to retraining, while recognising that family and work commitments could make participation difficult.

content.headline: Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack sues the Metropolitan Police
content.shortHeadline: Wrongly convicted Kenyan man says Met evidence destroyed his life
content.standfirst: Ali Kololo spent more than a decade in prison after being convicted over an attack on a British couple in Kenya. His conviction was quashed; he is now suing the Met over an officer’s evidence, a claim the force is contesting.

image.caption: Ali Kololo says his wrongful conviction and imprisonment destroyed his life.

sources.originalTitle: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple

segments.body: Ali Kololo says his life was destroyed after he was convicted in Kenya over the 2011 attack in which David Tebbutt was killed and his wife Judith abducted. Kololo spent more than a decade in prison before Kenya’s High Court quashed his conviction in 2023. He is now seeking compensation from the Metropolitan Police.

segments.title: Questions about the investigation
segments.body: The BBC reports that a Met officer, Neil Hibberd, relied on Kololo’s statement and footwear evidence at trial, despite the officer who arrested Kololo saying he was barefoot and the Met’s forensic examination being unable to link the shoe to marks at the scene. The UK’s police watchdog later found Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence; he had retired and could not face disciplinary proceedings.

Kololo says he was tortured by Kenyan police and is still struggling with the effects of prison and illness. The Met is contesting his claim and has declined to comment on its details. It said it remains committed to supporting Kenyan authorities in seeking justice for Judith Tebbutt and her late husband.

content.headline: Survey finds widespread racism and low confidence in UK workplace HR
content.shortHeadline: Nearly half of ethnic minority workers report workplace racism
content.standfirst: A survey found 45% of ethnic minority workers had experienced racism at work in the previous year, often dismissed as “banter”. More than half said they lacked confidence that HR would take their concerns seriously.

image.caption: The report’s authors say racism remains widespread in British life.

sources.originalTitle: Nearly half of ethnic minority people in UK have faced racism at work in last year, survey finds

segments.body: A survey of 2,506 adults from the UK’s five largest minority ethnic communities found that 75% had experienced racism or unfair treatment linked to race, ethnicity or religion in the previous year. Among ethnic minority workers, 45% reported workplace racism, and 56% had no confidence HR would take their concerns seriously.

segments.title: Reported effects on wellbeing
segments.body: Three-quarters of respondents who had experienced racism said it affected their mental health to some degree. Half said they felt they had to stay on guard for racist encounters, while only 5% sought professional mental-health support, according to the report.

The Race Equality Foundation said racism is shaped by wider political and social rhetoric as well as individual incidents. The survey reports that 42% of respondents who had faced racism linked it to anti-immigrant protests or demonstrations, while many said they frequently encountered negative posts about minorities online.

content.headline: Trump says Greenland agreement changed his view of NATO
content.shortHeadline: Trump says Greenland deal made him see NATO “a little differently”
content.standfirst: The US president again criticised NATO allies for not doing enough in the war against Iran, but said the Greenland agreement had altered his view. The deal allows two additional US bases while reaffirming the Danish realm’s sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.

image.caption: Donald Trump and Melania Trump answer reporters’ questions at Mar-a-Lago on Thanksgiving.

sources.originalTitle: Trump: Aftalen om Grønland fik mig til at se 'lidt anderledes på tingene'

segments.body: Donald Trump said the Greenland agreement made him see the situation “a little differently” after criticising NATO allies for not helping the US enough in the war against Iran. Asked about a possible reduction in US troops in Europe, he said he and NATO secretary general Mark Rutte had discussed it at length.

segments.title: What the agreement says
segments.body: The agreement, signed on 22 September, allows the US to establish two additional military bases in Greenland. It also reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and recognises Greenlanders as a people with a right to self-determination under international law.

content.headline: EU budget talks collapse early as Denmark and other states walk away
content.shortHeadline: EU budget summit ends early after Denmark and allies abandon talks
content.standfirst: Leaders ended negotiations a day early after a standoff between countries seeking a smaller EU budget and those defending farm and regional funds. Denmark and three other budget-restrictive states skipped late meetings; no agreement was reached.

image.caption: The EU summit on the next long-term budget was ended a day early.

sources.originalTitle: Forhandlingskollaps: Afbryder EU-topmøde en dag før tid
Kun 24 EU-lande stiller sig bag Ukraine-lån på topmøde

segments.body: EU leaders cut short a summit on the next long-term budget after talks stalled. Denmark, Sweden, Austria and Belgium—among the countries seeking to restrain spending—did not attend some late negotiating meetings. The summit ended without an agreement, and leaders are due to meet again in December.

segments.title: A divided bloc
segments.body: The seven budget-restrictive countries want a smaller overall budget and a greater share directed to new priorities such as security, competitiveness and the green transition. A group of 17 countries opposes cuts to agriculture and regional support. France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, also resisted reductions to farm subsidies.

Denmark’s finance ministry said the current proposal would increase the country’s EU contribution by DKK 12.1bn. Germany’s Friedrich Merz warned that countries refusing to support Ukraine could face consequences in future budget negotiations, but leaders did not agree on the wider budget at this summit.

content.headline: Documents suggest Denmark’s property appeals rule was designed to deter claims
content.shortHeadline: Records suggest property appeals rule was designed to limit complaints
content.standfirst: DR’s review of internal records says officials discussed ways to discourage appeals before the 20% rule was introduced. The tax minister says he is open to changes, but the rule’s intended use in cases involving plainly wrong information remains contested.

image.caption: DR’s reporting examines internal records on the property valuation appeals rule.

sources.originalTitle: Dokumenter afslører: For 11 år siden lagde topfolk en plan, der har konsekvenser for boligejere i dag

segments.body: Internal documents obtained by DR show tax officials discussing “complaint-prevention measures” while designing Denmark’s property valuation system in 2015. The records include proposals intended to reduce incentives to appeal; legal professor Rasmus Grønved Nielsen called the material striking and said the rule cuts into citizens’ normal appeal rights.

segments.title: How the threshold works
segments.body: Under the current rule, an appeal generally cannot change a valuation unless it is more than 20% wrong. DR reports that officials first discussed a 15% rule before a 20% threshold appeared in later documents. The system also taxes only 80% of the valuation as a safeguard against uncertainty.

The debate has intensified after a summer-home valuation used a building allowance far above the local plan’s limit. The tax authority acknowledged the error but did not change the valuation because the resulting difference was below 20%. Tax minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt says the tax agency should reconsider how the threshold applies when information is plainly incorrect; other appeals may still face the existing rule.

content.headline: Kerteminde council rejects Odense Port expansion plans
content.shortHeadline: Kerteminde council stops planning for Odense Port expansion
content.standfirst: A narrow council majority halted planning work for a proposed DKK 2bn expansion into Odense Fjord. Supporters say the port needs more space for green-industry production; opponents cite risks to nature and nearby communities.

image.caption: Residents celebrate after Kerteminde council voted against continuing port expansion planning.

sources.originalTitle: Havnedrama afgjort: 'Nu skal vi hjem og have champagne'

segments.body: Kerteminde’s council has voted to stop planning work for a proposed expansion of Odense Port, following a close vote. The plan would have added about one million square metres in Odense Fjord and included a new shipping channel. The port says it needs space to meet demand for production connected to the green transition.

segments.title: What divided the council
segments.body: Opponents raised concerns about the natural environment, small communities and the port’s relationship with its neighbours. Supporters said halting the work could mean lost business opportunities and harm the area’s reputation as a place to invest. The vote came after a new Social Democratic councillor joined those opposing continued planning.

content.headline: Antibiotic use in Danish animals rises again, led by pig farming
content.shortHeadline: Antibiotic use in Danish livestock rises, with pigs accounting for 84%
content.standfirst: New figures show antibiotic use in animals rose 1.14% in 2025 to 88.4 tonnes. A university lecturer warns that growing resistance—especially in pig production—could make human infections harder to treat.

image.caption: Pig farming accounts for about 84% of antibiotic use in animals in Denmark.

source.credit: Foto: Ida Marie Odgaard / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Antibiotikaforbruget til dyr fortsætter med at stige

segments.body: Antibiotic use in animals in Denmark rose 1.14% from 2024 to 2025, reaching 88.4 tonnes, according to figures from the State Serum Institute and the DTU National Food Institute. Pig production accounts for about 84% of the total.

segments.title: Resistance and farming practices
segments.body: The State Serum Institute says the increase has likely contributed to rising resistance in several bacteria monitored in pigs. Lecturer Dorte Frees says that resistance can undermine treatments relied on in surgery, cancer care and other parts of human medicine. She says use has increased again since a decline between 2013 and 2022.

The source says the EU’s 2022 ban on medicinal zinc oxide for animals may have contributed to greater antibiotic use, because zinc had been used to suppress bacterial growth. A political agreement set an ambition to reduce antibiotic use in pigs by 8% by 2027 compared with 2018; Frees says current trends are far from meeting it.

content.headline: Nyborg bans AI in social services after further case found
content.shortHeadline: Nyborg bans AI in social services after another breach of rules
content.standfirst: The municipality has halted AI use in its Social and Family department after finding another case where a tool was used in citizen-related work against its rules. A councillor says a broader investigation may be needed to establish how many cases were affected.

image.caption: Nyborg Municipality has stopped AI use in its Social and Family department.

sources.originalTitle: Efter brøler med kunstig intelligens: Nu forbyder kommune AI i socialsager

segments.body: Nyborg Municipality has banned the use of artificial intelligence across its Social and Family department after identifying at least one more case of AI being used in citizen-related casework against municipal rules. The decision follows an earlier apology after a caseworker used Copilot to speed up a resident’s appeal.

Municipal director Tim Jeppesen asked employees to review their AI prompts and report possible misuse. Councillor Martin Stenmann said the new case raises questions about how many files may be involved and that a more thorough investigation could be needed. The municipality declined DR’s request for an interview.

content.headline: Government to revise tax deal after concern over compensation payments
content.shortHeadline: Government to change tax deal affecting wrongful-dismissal payouts
content.standfirst: Ministers say they will exempt compensation for wrongful dismissal from a planned cut to tax-free allowances. The details remain unsettled, and a tax-law lecturer says distinguishing affected workers from other recipients could be difficult to administer.

image.caption: Government politicians presented the tax agreement in Copenhagen earlier this month.

sources.originalTitle: Regeringen vil ændre skatteaftale efter blot 14 dage: 'Det har aldrig været intentionen'

segments.body: The Danish government says it will change a tax agreement announced two weeks ago after unions warned it could increase tax on compensation for wrongful dismissal, including cases involving sexual harassment or unlawful dismissal during pregnancy. The agreement proposed cutting the tax-free threshold for certain payments from DKK 8,000 to DKK 1,000.

segments.title: The unresolved design
segments.body: SF tax spokesperson Sofie Lippert says officials are working on a way to exempt compensation for wrongful dismissals. HK union welcomed the reversal, saying the change could significantly reduce what affected workers receive. The government has not yet settled how the exemption will work.

Tax-law lecturer Anne Sofie Højrup Bondegaard says separating wrongful-dismissal compensation from other severance payments could require case-by-case decisions. She suggests retaining the existing threshold for severance payments generally and lowering it only for other categories, but that could reduce the tax revenue the reform was intended to raise.

content.headline: DKK 128m remains on discontinued anonymous travel cards
content.shortHeadline: Users must claim DKK 128m left on discontinued anonymous travel cards
content.standfirst: About 1.1 million users of Denmark’s anonymous Rejsekort still have DKK 128.4m in unused balances. Unlike balances on personal cards, the money cannot be refunded automatically; users have until 29 June 2027 to claim it.

image.caption: The physical Rejsekort system closed in June 2026; users can still claim remaining balances.

source.credit: Foto: Sebastian Elias Uth / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Rejsekort mangler at udbetale 128 millioner kroner

segments.body: Rejsekort & Rejseplan says DKK 128.4m remains on anonymous travel cards held by about 1.1 million people. The physical card system closed in June 2026, but anonymous cards are not linked to an individual, so users must request their balance themselves.

segments.title: How to claim the balance
segments.body: Users can apply through the Rejsekort & Rejseplan website or take their card to one of five listed service points. The deadline is 29 June 2027; any unclaimed money will be transferred to the regional public transport companies. So far, DKK 2.6m has been paid to 8,500 anonymous-card holders.

content.headline: Australia’s sandpapergate inquiry expands to include the 2017-18 Ashes
content.shortHeadline: Australia’s ball-tampering inquiry widens to include 2017-18 Ashes
content.standfirst: Cricket Australia’s independent forum will examine ball-management practices across the 2017-18 season, including the Ashes and the tour of South Africa that brought the scandal to light. It will not impose retrospective sanctions.

image.caption: Australia won the 2017-18 Ashes series against England 4-0.

sources.originalTitle: Australia's sandpapergate probe to also include 2017-18 Ashes

segments.body: Cricket Australia has widened its independent inquiry into the ball-tampering scandal to include the 2017-18 Ashes, which Australia won 4-0. Its remit covers ball-management practices across the men’s team that season, all four Tests on the subsequent South Africa tour and the investigation that followed.

segments.title: Disputed accounts
segments.body: The inquiry follows renewed scrutiny after former batter Usman Khawaja said in his autobiography that the team knew about the plan to tamper with the ball in the third Test in Cape Town. Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Pat Cummins have denied knowledge; Cummins called Khawaja’s account “nonsense”. David Warner and Cameron Bancroft have backed Khawaja’s version.

Everyone involved in the 2018 tour, including players and support staff, will be invited to give evidence, but participation is voluntary and information will be confidential unless a participant says otherwise. Cricket Australia says the forum will run for six weeks and it will publish the report and recommendations within 30 days of receiving them. No retrospective sanctions will be imposed.

content.headline: Ten-man Bournemouth make it five European wins in a row
content.shortHeadline: Ten-man Bournemouth extend record run to 10 wins
content.standfirst: Bournemouth came from behind at Celta Vigo after Bafodé Diakité’s first-half dismissal, winning their fifth European match in a row. The result also made it 10 consecutive wins in all competitions, a club record.

image.caption: Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose, who took over in the summer.

sources.originalTitle: Bournemouth 'allowed to dream' as fans book Europa League final hotels

segments.body: Bournemouth trailed to Iago Aspas’ goal and were reduced to 10 men when Bafodé Diakité was sent off midway through the first half. They still won at Celta Vigo, with second-half goals from Álvaro Rodríguez and Rayan completing the comeback. The Cherries have now won 10 matches in a row in all competitions, a club record.

segments.title: A European run to dream on
segments.body: Bournemouth are the only team to have won all five of their Europa League matches so far and sit top of the table. They are closing in on a top-eight finish, which would take them straight to the last 16 without a play-off. Alex Scott called winning the competition the team’s dream, while head coach Marco Rose said there were still many games to go.

content.headline: No post-match drug tests during South Africa-New Zealand rugby series
content.shortHeadline: No post-match drug tests during Springboks-All Blacks series
content.standfirst: Anti-doping authorities conducted no post-match tests during the four-Test series, despite such testing being standard at many elite fixtures. World Rugby pointed to its year-round testing programme but did not confirm the reported absence of tests.

image.caption: The Springboks and All Blacks played three Tests in South Africa and a fourth in Baltimore.

sources.originalTitle: No post-match drug testing in South Africa v New Zealand series

segments.body: South Africa and New Zealand players were not given a single post-match drugs test during their four-Test series in August and September, BBC Sport reports. The matches took place in South Africa apart from the final Test in Baltimore. The series agreement referred to World Rugby’s anti-doping rules, but post-match testing was not carried out.

segments.title: The wider testing picture
segments.body: World Rugby did not confirm the absence of tests in the series. It said its risk-based, no-notice programme tests players throughout the year, including during international windows; South Africa’s anti-doping body referred questions back to World Rugby. The report also notes that South Africa’s testing body recorded 225 rugby tests in its latest annual report, down from 753 a decade earlier, and says overseas laboratory costs have risen.

content.headline: Germany forward Laura Freigang banned for 16 months over testing failures
content.shortHeadline: Freigang banned for 16 months after three testing failures
content.standfirst: Germany and Eintracht Frankfurt forward Laura Freigang has been suspended over three reporting and/or testing failures. The ban rules her out of next summer’s Women’s World Cup and sidelines her from football activity until after 7 October 2027.

image.caption: Germany forward Laura Freigang has scored 17 goals in 45 appearances for her country.

sources.originalTitle: Germany's Freigang banned over drugs test issues

segments.body: Laura Freigang has been suspended for 16 months after a dispute-resolution agreement with the German Football Association, the World Anti-Doping Agency and Germany’s National Anti-Doping Agency. The case concerns three reporting and/or testing failures between 11 March 2025 and 23 February 2026. She can return to training two months before the ban ends, but cannot play until after 7 October 2027.

segments.title: Impact on club and country
segments.body: The suspension means Freigang will miss next summer’s Women’s World Cup. Her personal records for appearances, goals, assists and other statistics from 23 February 2026 have been nullified, although Eintracht Frankfurt’s results are unaffected. She has scored six goals and made two assists in 11 league starts this season. The club says it will discuss the terms of her future employment with her.

content.headline: Great Britain beat Germany to reach Davis Cup semi-finals
content.shortHeadline: Patten and Skupski seal Great Britain’s Davis Cup semi-final place
content.standfirst: Henry Patten and Neal Skupski won the deciding doubles match to send Great Britain past third seeds Germany in Bologna. The team reaches the last four for the first time since 2019 and will face Spain on Saturday.

image.caption: Henry Patten and Neal Skupski celebrate their doubles win over Germany.

sources.originalTitle: GB win decider to reach Davis Cup semi-finals

segments.body: Cameron Norrie put Great Britain ahead with a three-set win over Jan-Lennard Struff, before Alexander Zverev beat Arthur Fery to take the tie to a deciding doubles match. Patten and Skupski then defeated Kevin Krawietz and Tim Pütz 6-2 7-6 (8-6), saving five break points in the first set and recovering from a mini-break down in the tie-break.

segments.title: A first semi-final since 2019
segments.body: The win puts Great Britain in the Davis Cup semi-finals for the first time since 2019. Patten and Skupski, who are set to partner up for the 2027 season, have won all three of their Davis Cup matches together. They are scheduled to face Spain on Saturday; Spain’s singles wins meant Carlos Alcaraz did not need to play in the quarter-final, though captain David Ferrer said he could be in contention for the semi-final.

content.headline: Camilo Duran’s late winner keeps Celtic’s Europa League hopes alive
content.shortHeadline: Duran strikes late to keep Celtic’s European campaign alive
content.standfirst: Camilo Duran came off the bench to head Celtic past Portuguese second-tier side Torreense, continuing a prolific season and keeping the club within reach of a Europa League play-off place. The performance also renewed questions about the team’s wider struggles.

image.caption: Camilo Duran has scored 15 goals this season for a Celtic side pursuing European progress.

sources.originalTitle: 'Priceless' Duran proves 'the man' but is he papering over cracks at Celtic?

segments.body: Celtic were labouring against Torreense until Camilo Duran came on with just over half an hour remaining and scored a late winner. The 24-year-old has now scored 15 goals and provided six assists in 23 appearances this season. Manager Martin O’Neill called him “priceless” and said he had taken on the role of “the man”.

segments.title: More than one player’s burden
segments.body: Duran’s goals have helped keep Celtic within reach of a Europa League play-off place with three fixtures remaining, and have also proved decisive in domestic matches. But the report describes a side short of attacking ideas against Torreense, with limited contributions from several players and no driving force in midfield. Celtic remain only a point clear of Rangers, and the account argues that Duran may need to sustain his form if the club are to progress.

content.headline: Former England scrum-half and rugby commentator Nigel Starmer-Smith dies at 81
content.shortHeadline: Nigel Starmer-Smith, former England player and commentator, dies at 81
content.standfirst: Starmer-Smith made seven appearances for England before a long career in broadcasting, including 15 years voicing the BBC’s Rugby Special. His son said he died peacefully after a long battle with dementia.

image.caption: Nigel Starmer-Smith voiced the BBC’s rugby highlights programme Rugby Special for 15 years.

sources.originalTitle: Former England scrum-half Starmer-Smith dies aged 81

segments.body: Nigel Starmer-Smith, former England scrum-half and rugby union commentator, has died aged 81. He represented Harlequins and the Barbarians and played seven times for England between 1969 and 1971. After retiring in 1976, he became a broadcaster and journalist, voicing the BBC’s Rugby Special for 15 years and commentating for ITV at the 2003 Rugby World Cup.

segments.title: Remembered by his family
segments.body: Starmer-Smith had been diagnosed with dementia in 2015. His son Charlie said he died peacefully after a long battle with the condition, which he said had robbed his father of his ability to communicate. He remembered him as a rugby player, commentator, writer, fundraiser and family man, and asked those who knew him to remember a happy moment and smile.

content.headline: Selby starts UK Championship defence against Matt Selt
content.shortHeadline: Selby draws Selt as UK Championship begins on Saturday
content.standfirst: Mark Selby opens his title defence against Matt Selt at the UK Championship in York. Ronnie O’Sullivan faces Jack Lisowski, while Mark Allen is set to return to the tournament after a five-month break from the sport.

image.caption: Mark Selby is defending his UK Championship title in York.

sources.originalTitle: Selby faces tough UK opener while Allen set to feature

segments.body: Four-time world champion Mark Selby begins his UK Championship title defence against Matt Selt on Saturday. Selt reached the televised stages by beating Jak Jones, the highest-ranked player in qualifying. The tournament, the season’s first Triple Crown event, runs from 28 November to 6 December at York Barbican, with a top prize of £312,500.

segments.title: A notable return and a marquee tie
segments.body: Ronnie O’Sullivan has been drawn against Jack Lisowski, who set up the match with a 6-4 qualifying win over Mark Joyce. Mark Allen is set to face Yuan Sijun after returning to the sport following five months away; he lost to Jordan Brown in his first-round match at the Northern Ireland Open in October. Allen spoke publicly about mental health struggles last month.

content.headline: Andy Taylor’s rock guitar helped define Duran Duran’s sound
content.shortHeadline: Andy Taylor’s guitar gave Duran Duran a harder edge
content.standfirst: The guitarist, who has died aged 65, brought a rock sensibility to the band’s polished pop. His playing helped turn synth-led songs into hits with an appeal beyond the group’s original New Romantic world.

image.caption: Andy Taylor in Maison Rouge Studios in 1984.

sources.originalTitle: Andy Taylor, guitarist in Duran Duran, dies aged 65
Duran Duran were transformed by Andy Taylor’s rock edge – and never quite the same without him

segments.body: Andy Taylor, Duran Duran’s guitarist, has died aged 65. Diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, he disclosed his illness in 2022. The band said his playing brought an “indelible fire and swagger” to the songs that took them around the world.

segments.title: A rock edge in a pop band
segments.body: Taylor’s harder-rock influences set him apart from his bandmates, but his guitar helped give Duran Duran a distinctive sound. The Guardian’s account argues that it also made their synth-heavy pop more accessible to US radio, helping the group become a major British success in America.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s retrospective focuses on Taylor’s musical role: his guitar translated some of Nick Rhodes’s synth ideas into a rock language and, the article argues, gave US radio programmers a familiar point of entry.

content.headline: Novelist’s eclectic Scenes confirms him as a British rap original
content.shortHeadline: Novelist’s genre-hopping Scenes is a confident return
content.standfirst: Eight years after his debut album, the south London rapper packs 25 tracks into a restless, 45-minute record. The review hears sharp writing and a fearless range of styles held together by his distinctive voice.

image.caption: South London rapper Novelist, also known as Kojo Kankam.

sources.originalTitle: Novelist’s first album in eight years has Skepta, skits and soul – and showcases a true British original

segments.body: Scenes moves between grime, soul, jungle, baile funk and skits, refusing to settle into one sound. The Guardian review finds coherence instead in Novelist’s sharp, unsentimental rhymes and his willingness to follow each musical idea wherever it leads.

segments.title: A world beyond the album
segments.body: The release comes with an air freshener and a small driving game set around London and Los Angeles landmarks. The review treats these eccentric extras as part of Novelist’s independent-minded approach, rather than a substitute for the music.

content.headline: The KLF-backed People’s Pyramid turns grief into a public ritual
content.shortHeadline: Birkenhead’s People’s Pyramid makes mourning communal
content.standfirst: At the annual Day of the Dead in Birkenhead, families add bricks containing glazed ashes to a growing monument. The event mixes noise, celebration and reflection, and has become a community its organisers say extends beyond the KLF’s original involvement.

image.caption: Participants carry out the Krossing of the Dark Park at Birkenhead’s Day of the Dead.

sources.originalTitle: ‘My brother was its first body’: would you add your corpse to Birkenhead’s pyramid of dead people?

segments.body: The People’s Pyramid is planned to contain 34,592 bricks, each holding a small portion of someone’s cremated remains. At this year’s ceremony, mourners processed through Birkenhead Park, added new bricks and called out the names of the dead amid music, foghorns and a collective moment of noise.

segments.title: A community built around remembrance
segments.body: For participants, the event offers a recurring place to remember people whose funerals did not feel like the right tribute. Families return each year, and organisers hope the monument may eventually have a permanent home in Birkenhead Park. Funding remains uncertain.

content.headline: The Damned mark 50 years with a ferocious, shape-shifting set
content.shortHeadline: The Damned’s 50th-anniversary show stays gloriously unruly
content.standfirst: With all their surviving original members onstage, the punk veterans ranged from hardcore-speed blasts to goth theatrics and prog detours. The review finds their eclecticism still bound together by the force of the performance.

image.caption: Dave Vanian performs with the Damned at Brighton Dome.

sources.originalTitle: Mwhahaha! After 50 years, the Damned are still an outrageously fun blast of punk, pop and gothic camp

segments.body: Rather than rely on a set of early punk hits, the Damned drew on the many directions their music took afterwards. The Guardian’s Brighton review highlights the hardcore charge of “Love Song”, the horror-show camp of “Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde” and a knowingly expansive “Curtain Call”.

The variety never loosens the show’s grip. At 70, Dave Vanian’s baritone remains striking, while the band attacks even the half-century-old “New Rose” with the urgency of new material. Their longevity, the review suggests, has not tamed their messy, contrarian appeal.

content.headline: Bob Dylan’s voice surprises at 85 as he reworks his songs again
content.shortHeadline: Bob Dylan’s voice is a surprise on his latest UK tour
content.standfirst: Opening another UK leg of his Never Ending Tour, Dylan offered no stage chat and little concession to nostalgia. The review finds imaginative arrangements, an unexpectedly strong voice and moments when the slow pace drifts.

image.caption: Bob Dylan performing in 2023.

sources.originalTitle: Bob Dylan review – at 85, he is in finer voice now than he was 40 years ago

segments.body: Dylan performed from behind a piano, guiding his band through a two-hour set with minimal lighting and no gaps between songs. Familiar material arrived in altered forms: “Tangled Up in Blue” became subdued jazz, while “It Ain’t Me Babe” received a probing, delicate arrangement.

segments.title: A voice with new force
segments.body: The reviewer says Dylan’s voice was the evening’s surprise: robust, powerful and clearer than it had sounded four decades earlier. Some slower songs approached lounge music, but the performance’s lyrical sharpness and a closing “I Shall Be Released” offered a route back to the songs for listeners seeking familiar ground.

content.headline: Morten Harket on Parkinson’s, fame and making a new a-ha-free album
content.shortHeadline: Morten Harket on Parkinson’s, fame and Human Grace
content.standfirst: The a-ha singer says medication side effects have affected his access to singing and guitar, but he describes his Parkinson’s diagnosis as a forceful pause rather than a devastation. His new album also features his daughters on two tracks.

image.caption: a-ha frontman Morten Harket.

sources.originalTitle: a-ha’s Morten Harket: ‘My Parkinson’s diagnosis wasn’t devastating. I have a new appreciation for the human organism’

segments.body: Morten Harket says Parkinson’s medication has affected his ability to sing and play guitar. For Human Grace, he and his collaborators drew on older recordings of his voice. He describes the diagnosis as having stopped his previous life and made him newly appreciative of the body’s “architecture”.

segments.title: Fame and family
segments.body: In the interview, Harket recalls the precarious early days of a-ha in south London, when the band slept in cramped, unsafe accommodation, and reflects on the isolation fame brought. He also explains that his daughters’ contributions to two songs were unplanned, after the tracks seemed to need additional voices.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s solo debut brings old folk songs into striking new forms
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat’s solo debut makes folk feel newly alive
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer draws on Irish, British and American song traditions for an album shaped around her commanding contralto. Its most adventurous turn recasts a folk tune as a dark, widescreen trip-hop piece.

sources.originalTitle: No Human Tongue Can Tell

segments.body: No Human Tongue Can Tell keeps Radie Peat’s voice at its centre, whether she sings alone or builds choruses from her own layers. The Pitchfork review praises the way her arrangements move across time and tradition without losing the clarity and force of her singing.

segments.title: Tradition with room to change
segments.body: Peat selects songs featuring women negotiating limited choices, then reshapes them with keyboards, concertina and electronic textures. On “The Moon and Stars”, a fiddle tune becomes a trip-hop composition that the review calls the album’s most powerful transformation.

content.headline: Glastonbury’s 2027 headliners are strong names but a cautious choice
content.shortHeadline: Glastonbury’s 2027 bill is short on surprise
content.standfirst: Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender have all earned headline status, the i argues, but their similar career stages make for an underwhelming trio. The piece points to fee limits and the festival’s changing cultural pull as part of the problem.

image.caption: Harry Styles, one of Glastonbury’s announced 2027 Pyramid Stage headliners.

sources.originalTitle: Why Glastonbury can’t get good headliners

segments.body: The i’s critic argues that Glastonbury’s announced Pyramid Stage headliners for 2027—Styles, Eilish and Fender—are individually credible but collectively too similar. The complaint is not about their talent; it is that the festival has chosen little risk or contrast for its most prominent slots.

segments.title: The limits of the booking power
segments.body: The article suggests that Glastonbury’s reported maximum headline fee of £500,000 makes it harder to attract some major touring acts, while the festival’s shared spotlight may also deter established stars. It questions whether the event still has the cultural leverage it once did.

content.headline: Gérard Depardieu will face trial over an alleged rape in Paris
content.shortHeadline: Depardieu ordered to face trial over alleged rape
content.standfirst: An appeals court has upheld a trial over one alleged 2018 rape accusation by actor Charlotte Arnould, while dismissing a second allegation. Depardieu denies wrongdoing and his lawyer is considering a further appeal.

image.caption: Gérard Depardieu at a public appearance.

sources.originalTitle: ⁠Gérard Depardieu to face trial on charges ‌of raping ​actor Charlotte ⁠Arnould

segments.body: The court ruled that Gérard Depardieu should stand trial over an alleged rape of Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in August 2018. It dismissed a separate allegation said to have occurred the following week. Depardieu denies wrongdoing; the trial date has not been supplied.

segments.title: A separate conviction remains
segments.body: The ruling follows Depardieu’s decision to drop an appeal against a 2025 conviction for sexually assaulting two film-set workers; his 18-month suspended sentence stands. His lawyer called the latest decision a “first victory” for Depardieu while saying the legal process is not finished.

content.headline: Julie Delpy on predatory directors, anger and making her own films
content.shortHeadline: Julie Delpy on anger, agency and a life in film
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and director discusses harassment she says she faced as a young performer, the struggle to receive credit for her work and an industry she believes has tried to keep her down. She is writing six screenplays and says she is excited about what comes next.

image.caption: Julie Delpy at home in West Hollywood.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors

segments.body: Julie Delpy recalls being asked to undress by a director when she was 13 and describes other experiences of harassment in her career. She says that refusing a powerful director’s advances in her early 20s was followed by word spreading that she was “difficult”.

segments.title: Making work on her own terms
segments.body: Delpy says she contributed ideas and dialogue to Before Sunrise but was frustrated not to receive a writing credit. She later shared a writing credit on Before Sunset. Now writing several screenplays, she says directing and writing let her turn ideas into something tangible, even if not every project succeeds.

content.headline: An Eye for an Eye complicates the story of justice and victimhood in Iran
content.shortHeadline: An Iranian documentary challenges easy ideas of justice
content.standfirst: Tanaz Eshaghian discusses her film about Tahereh, a woman facing execution unless she can meet her husband’s family’s demand for blood money after killing him. The documentary also asks what happens when a woman’s story defies expectations of a “perfect victim”.

image.caption: A still from An Eye for an Eye, directed by Tanaz Eshaghian and Farzad Jafari.

sources.originalTitle: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice

segments.body: Under Iran’s penal code, the heirs of a murder victim can seek execution, financial compensation or forgiveness. An Eye for an Eye follows Tahereh, who is out on bail after killing her husband and faces execution unless she can raise the compensation demanded by his family.

segments.title: A story that resists simple answers
segments.body: Co-director Tanaz Eshaghian describes a film that does not present Tahereh as an uncomplicated victim: the killing was premeditated, and questions remain about what happened. The documentary also records her account of years of violence and the lack of help she found, while exploring the women on both sides of the case.

content.headline: The Fox review: Olivia Colman leads a wonderfully odd Australian fable
content.shortHeadline: The Fox is a peculiar, playful fable with Olivia Colman
content.standfirst: Dario Russo’s debut sends a talking fox, a troubled couple and a magical hole into a comic spiral. The review enjoys its retro texture and strange transformations, finding more flair here than in a similar recent film.

image.caption: Jai Courtney as Nick and Emily Browning as Kori in The Fox.

sources.originalTitle: The Fox review – talking animals are the least weird thing in this delightfully peculiar comedy

segments.body: In a small Australian town, Nick turns to a talking fox for advice after learning his girlfriend is having an affair. The fox tells him to push her into a magical hole so she will emerge loyal. The Guardian review describes the film as a retro-styled, off-kilter fairytale in which this choice takes the story somewhere increasingly strange.

Olivia Colman voices the fox, while Emily Browning, Jai Courtney and the late Sam Neill help establish the film’s peculiar comic tone. The review praises its visual atmosphere and the way it lets its odd premise unfold without giving away where the plot goes.

content.headline: Amanda Seyfried says You Can See Everything kept her in the dark
content.shortHeadline: Amanda Seyfried on joining You Can See Everything
content.standfirst: Seyfried says Nathan Fielder brought her into the Elizabeth Holmes documentary late, with access to its footage and script tightly controlled. She recalls being filmed as she watched material and wondering how she had ended up inside the project.

image.caption: Amanda Seyfried, who played Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout and appeared in You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: Amanda Seyfried needed ‘five-factor authentication’ to read You Can See Everything script but still ‘told everyone’

segments.body: Amanda Seyfried says Nathan Fielder first contacted her to discuss her portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout. He later asked her to watch footage for You Can See Everything on camera. She says she could not see the film’s material until she was on set and sometimes received the script only the night before.

Seyfried recalls a dinner with Fielder and Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, as a “Twilight Zone” experience: she was in his home with Holmes’s children and a camera crew, questioning whether she had become too involved. The documentary has since become a major box-office success in North America.

content.headline: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie settle their dispute over Château Miraval
content.shortHeadline: Pitt and Jolie settle winery dispute
content.standfirst: The former couple have agreed to end their legal battle over the French winery they once owned together. The terms are confidential; claims about the sale and allegations raised in the dispute remain contested in the reporting.

image.caption: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt at the 2015 WSJ Magazine Innovator Awards.

sources.originalTitle: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie settle years-long legal battle over joint French winery

segments.body: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled their legal dispute over Château Miraval, according to a joint statement. Both sides have moved to dismiss claims against each other, and the terms of the agreement have not been made public.

Pitt sued after Jolie sold her stake to the Stoli Group, arguing she had broken an agreement not to sell without his consent. Jolie’s counterclaim described alleged abuse and said negotiations over her share foundered over a proposed nondisclosure agreement. Pitt denied the accusations.

content.headline: Wicker review: Olivia Colman’s twig-built romance is strange and funny
content.shortHeadline: Wicker is a strange, funny tale of a husband made of twigs
content.standfirst: An isolated fisherwoman commissions a husband woven from willow in this bawdy, deliberately lopsided fairy tale. The review questions its treatment of the husband’s agency but finds a comic fantasy in its reversal of familiar gender expectations.

image.caption: Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman pays for a husband woven from wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, a fisherwoman played by Olivia Colman pays a basketmaker to create her a husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård, from willow. The resulting romance brings comic absurdity to a village where women’s lives are constrained by convention.

segments.title: A fairy tale with an uneasy bargain
segments.body: The reviewer sees a real tension in the film’s fantasy: the wicker husband’s devotion is written as a joke and a wish fulfilment, but his freedom is difficult to separate from the fact that his wife paid for his creation. The review ultimately enjoys the film’s bawdy tone while arguing its equality message is simpler than its provocation.

content.headline: Don’t Look Back in Anger celebrates Oasis’s reunion but skips the story
content.shortHeadline: Oasis reunion film delivers the euphoria, not the explanation
content.standfirst: Steven Knight’s documentary finds moving scenes of fans around the world and captures the Gallagher brothers’ renewed warmth. But the review says it avoids the central questions of how the reunion happened and what repaired their relationship.

image.caption: A still from Steven Knight’s documentary about the Oasis reunion tour.

sources.originalTitle: Oasis fans’ most important question remains unanswered

segments.body: The film follows Oasis on their 2025 reunion tour, from rehearsals to crowds across several countries. The i review praises the concert footage and the emotional response of fans, including a new generation drawn to songs written decades earlier.

segments.title: The missing middle
segments.body: The documentary moves from a brief history of the band’s split to rehearsals, leaving out much of the intervening years and the reconciliation itself. The review also notes that it barely addresses ticket pricing, leaving its uplifting account of forgiveness without the explanation viewers may be seeking.

content.headline: Tulisa’s The Reckoning turns a tabloid sting into a call for change
content.shortHeadline: Tulisa’s documentary looks beyond the 2013 sting
content.standfirst: The three-part series revisits the Sun on Sunday’s fake-film audition sting and Tulisa Contostavlos’s arrest, then follows her campaign for tighter media regulation. The review praises her advocacy but says the programme’s scope sometimes blurs the questions it wants answered.

image.caption: Tulisa Contostavlos in The Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: Tulisa: The Reckoning review – it’s hard to believe how far the disgusting drugs set-up went

segments.body: Tulisa: The Reckoning recounts how the singer was drawn into a supposed film audition and then asked to supply drugs to a producer, leading to her arrest and a trial that later collapsed. She says the experience contributed to a suicide attempt in 2013.

segments.title: Campaigning after the scandal
segments.body: The series follows Tulisa as she meets campaigners and politicians and calls for stronger media regulation. The Guardian review values her resolve but says the documentary takes on so much—including other episodes of press intrusion—that it does not fully test what reforms would make the greatest difference. IPSO disputes the programme’s criticism of its independence and handling of complaints.

content.headline: The Hunting Wives finds a wide audience in its Texas culture clash
content.shortHeadline: The Hunting Wives mixes Texas culture wars with soap
content.standfirst: The Netflix drama returns with more sex, scandal and a murder investigation, but its appeal is not limited to its provocative surface. Critics and Texas observers discuss its satire of political performance and the varied views of the state it depicts.

sources.originalTitle: 'It appeals across demographics': How steamy soap The Hunting Wives took on sex, scandal and the US's blue-red divide

segments.body: The Hunting Wives centres on an affluent east Texas community and the affair between East Coast liberal Sophie and conservative powerbroker Margo. Its second season leans into the show’s mix of erotic melodrama, secrets and partisan friction; Netflix has already confirmed a third season.

segments.title: Beyond the political labels
segments.body: Time critic Judy Berman says the show’s characters are preoccupied with political image as much as ethics, helping explain its cross-demographic appeal. Texas Monthly editor Taylor Prewitt adds that the state’s residents often encounter people with opposing views in daily life, a dynamic the show uses for teasing and conflict.

perspectives.body: Prewitt’s Texas-based perspective distinguishes the show’s heightened soap opera from its depiction of a state where people with differing political views often have to interact.

content.headline: Top Gear’s Gordon Ramsay reboot needs more than a famous host
content.shortHeadline: Can Gordon Ramsay give Top Gear a lasting reboot?
content.standfirst: The BBC plans to revive the motoring show in 2028 with Ramsay as lead host, but has not announced his co-presenters. The coverage weighs his car knowledge and television experience against the show’s history of short-lived celebrity-led line-ups.

image.caption: Gordon Ramsay, announced as the lead host of the Top Gear revival.

sources.originalTitle: Top Gear to return with Gordon Ramsay as lead host
‘Big names are notoriously flighty’: will Gordon Ramsay save Top Gear – and can he handle the drudgery?

segments.body: BBC Studios says filming for the new Top Gear will take place next year, with the series due to air in 2028 at Dunsfold aerodrome. Ramsay, a car enthusiast who has appeared on the programme as a guest, will lead the presenting team; the BBC says familiar features including the Stig will return.

segments.title: The challenge is continuity
segments.body: The Guardian’s analysis argues that a big name may attract viewers but may not want the regular work of a long-running magazine show. It says the as-yet-unnamed co-hosts will be crucial to giving the revival stability if Ramsay leaves. Richard Hammond, approached about returning, said he did not want to take Top Gear back to what it was.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis focuses less on Ramsay’s suitability than on the risk of building the reboot around a celebrity who may not stay, and the need for co-presenters who can sustain it.

content.headline: I Am Helen shifts the focus from toxic men to their partners
content.shortHeadline: I Am Helen shows the cost of a partner’s misogyny
content.standfirst: Nicola Coughlan plays a woman whose partner’s coercive behaviour grows out of everyday attitudes as much as overt hostility. The review argues that the drama’s attention to the woman living with that behaviour fills a gap in television’s depictions of toxic masculinity.

image.caption: Nicola Coughlan as Helen and Joe Cole as Steve in I Am Helen.

sources.originalTitle: All men should watch I Am Helen

segments.body: In the latest instalment of Dominic Savage’s anthology, Helen’s partner Steve begins choking her during sex without consent. He then presents himself as the injured party. The i review says the scene’s force lies in how quickly the relationship slips back toward normal after the incident.

segments.title: The ordinary roots of harm
segments.body: The review traces Steve’s changing attitudes to casual workplace talk that tells him he is being denied what he deserves. It argues that Helen’s perspective shifts attention from men’s self-image to the women who bear the consequences, without suggesting that the drama’s subject is simple.

content.headline: Open Secret examines how Russell Brand’s behaviour was enabled
content.shortHeadline: Open Secret looks at the culture that enabled Brand
content.standfirst: The Netflix documentary brings together reporting, testimony and old footage after Brand was sentenced for rape and sexual assault. The review says its most disturbing argument is not that his conduct was invisible, but that it could be treated as acceptable.

image.caption: A still from Netflix’s documentary about Russell Brand.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Russell Brand documentary feels like a horror film

segments.body: Open Secret draws on the Sunday Times investigation and includes accounts from comedians, former partners and people who knew Russell Brand. The i review says the programme’s effect comes from seeing earlier footage alongside later testimony and the conduct described by those interviewed.

segments.title: The wider culture
segments.body: The review argues that Brand’s behaviour was often visible in the entertainment culture around him, where he was framed as a playboy or provocative comic. It says the documentary’s indictment reaches beyond one individual to the institutions and audiences that made his persona commercially acceptable.

content.headline: Prue and Sandi’s South African trip is a joyful travelogue with depth
content.shortHeadline: Prue and Sandi’s South Africa trip finds joy and memory
content.standfirst: Prue Leith returns to places from her childhood with former Bake Off colleague Sandi Toksvig. The review delights in their friendship while noting the series’ franker moments of reflection on apartheid and the changes Leith has witnessed.

image.caption: Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig in Simon’s Town, South Africa.

sources.originalTitle: Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure review – you’ll feel lucky to have this joyful show in your life

segments.body: The six-part series follows Leith and Toksvig around South Africa, with Leith sharing memories of the country she left at 20. The Guardian review finds much of its charm in their contrasting rhythms: Leith’s recollections and Toksvig’s exuberant curiosity.
